parts: Holds nearly all the atom's mass
processes: Being the dense center of the atom
plainLanguageExplanation: The nucleus is the core of the atom — the tiny, dense, positively charged blob at the very center. Everything that gives the atom its mass is jammed in there: the protons and neutrons. Here is the mind-bending part: the nucleus is incredibly small. If an atom were a football stadium, the nucleus would be a marble on the center spot. The rest of the stadium — the enormous space around that marble — is where the electrons orbit. Yet despite being so tiny, the nucleus holds nearly all of the atom's mass. A proton or neutron weighs about 1,836 times more than an electron, so the few protons and neutrons in the nucleus outweigh all the electrons put together. The nucleus also carries the atom's positive charge — the protons inside it. That positive charge is what reaches out across the empty space and pulls the negative electrons in, keeping the whole atom together. The nucleus is small, dense, positive, and the center of everything in chemistry.

whyItMatters: The nucleus is where an atom's identity and nearly all its mass live. It explains why atoms are mostly empty space, why the periodic table orders elements by proton count, and — at the extreme — why nuclear energy is so powerful: the nucleus is a bundle of enormous energy and force.
tagline: The dense heart of the atom
didYouKnow: If you squeezed all the empty space out of your body — shrinking it to just the nuclei of its atoms — you would be smaller than a grain of sand.
compareReason: The nucleus and the shells are the two halves of atomic structure — comparing the dense core with the vast empty space around it makes the atom's true anatomy unforgettable.
